title: When AI Agents Get the Answer Wrong
summary: AI agents fail less often at the reasoning layer than at the tool-calling layer, where a website returns an unexpected result and the agent presents it confidently as fact anyway. The gap between confidence and correctness is the real reliability problem, and closing it requires better error detection across the entire system, not just a smarter model.
body_markdown:
AI tools are often described in extremes. They are either presented as revolutionary systems that will transform how we work, or dismissed as unreliable technologies that are not ready for serious use.


After spending the past two weeks testing Instinct, I found a more complicated reality. The tool is a good example of how AI can be **underrated and overrated at the same time** .


It can make everyday tasks noticeably easier. It can also produce confident, incorrect answers that reveal a deeper problem with the way AI agents interact with the web.


## The practical value of AI agents


Some of the most useful AI experiences are not necessarily the most dramatic ones.


Instinct has made weekend errands much simpler for me. Tasks that would normally involve opening several tabs, comparing options, reading reviews, and checking details can often be handled more quickly through a single conversational interface.


That convenience matters. Research is often less about one difficult question and more about a series of small decisions. Which option is best? What are the relevant tradeoffs? What information is missing? Which sources are worth trusting?


When an AI agent can help organize that process, it reduces the time and effort required to reach a decision. The result may not feel futuristic, but it is genuinely useful.


This is where AI agents can be underrated. They are not always changing the world in obvious ways, but they can quietly remove friction from ordinary activities.


## Where the experience breaks down


The limitations become clearer in more complex use cases, especially when an agent has to interact with multiple websites or external tools.


Instinct performs particularly well for certain high-value tasks, such as finding flights for an upcoming business trip. In those situations, the agent can coordinate research across different sources and present the results in a useful way.


However, the same system can also produce what users commonly describe as hallucinations.


In one example, the problem was not that the underlying language model misunderstood a piece of information. Instead, **the failure happened during a tool call** . The agent interacted with an external site incorrectly, received an unexpected result, and then presented that result confidently as though it were accurate.


From the user's perspective, the distinction may not matter. The answer is still wrong.


**The model may be functioning as designed, but the overall system has failed.**


The user does not experience the model, browser, tool, or website as separate components. They experience one AI assistant that gave them an incorrect answer.


## The growing importance of tool calling


As AI agents become more capable, they increasingly depend on tools. They search websites, retrieve information, fill out forms, compare products, make reservations, and pass data between systems.


Every additional tool introduces another point where something can go wrong.


A website may return information in an unexpected format. A page may change its structure. A tool may interpret an instruction differently than intended. An agent may select the wrong field, misunderstand a result, or continue operating after an earlier step has already failed.


These errors are especially difficult because the final response can still sound clear and authoritative.


That creates a dangerous **gap between confidence and correctness** . The user may assume that a polished answer reflects a successful chain of actions, even when the chain included a failure that was never detected or communicated.


The challenge is not only improving the model. It is also improving the systems around the model so that errors are identified, explained, and contained.


## The web is changing around AI agents


The problem becomes more significant as websites evolve to treat AI agents differently from human users.


Some sites may provide different experiences to automated systems. Others may introduce restrictions, alternative interfaces, or new verification steps. Even when these changes are intended to protect users or prevent abuse, they can create unexpected behavior for agents.


As more websites adapt to the presence of AI, tool-calling errors may become more common rather than less common. An agent could receive a response that looks valid but means something different from what it expects. It could be redirected to a page that changes the task's context. It could complete only part of an operation while reporting success.


These failures accumulate across the entire workflow.


The user, however, sees only the final answer. If the result is wrong, the user is left with a bad experience and little visibility into what happened behind the scenes.


## Building trust requires more than better answers


AI agents will not earn trust simply by becoming more fluent or more confident. They need to become better at **recognizing uncertainty and reporting failures** .


An agent should be able to distinguish between information it verified successfully and information it inferred from an incomplete tool response. It should know when an external action did not complete as expected. It should communicate uncertainty instead of turning a failed process into a confident conclusion.


This does not mean AI agents need to be perfect before they are useful. Instinct demonstrates that even imperfect systems can provide meaningful value.


It does mean that **reliability must be measured across the entire agent experience** , not only through the quality of the language model's response. Tool selection, website compatibility, error handling, verification, and transparency all contribute to whether an answer deserves to be trusted.


## Conclusion


AI agents are already useful in ways that are easy to overlook. They can simplify research, reduce repetitive work, and make everyday decisions faster.


At the same time, their weaknesses reveal an important lesson. Many incorrect answers are not caused by the model alone. They emerge from the interaction between the model, its tools, and the changing websites it depends on.


As agents take on more responsibility, these systems will need stronger safeguards around tool calling and clearer ways to communicate failure.


**The future of AI agents will not be determined only by how intelligently they can respond. It will also depend on how reliably they can act, how honestly they can report what happened, and how effectively they can prevent a small tool error from becoming a confident wrong answer.**
